propositions.text: Fengling Xu and Min Jin Yang are married with a son Jie Tao Yang; all seek protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97.
propositions.quote: Fengling Xu and Min Jin Yang are a married couple. Jie Tao Yang is their son. All three have sought protection in Canada under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA].

propositions.text: Ms. Xu fears persecution in China as a Falun Gong practitioner and due to family planning practices.
propositions.quote: Ms. Xu claims to fear persecution in China, her country of nationality, because she is a Falun Gong practitioner and because of that country’s oppressive family planning practices.

propositions.text: Mr. Yang fears persecution in Guyana due to ethnicity and claims protection need.
propositions.quote: Mr. Yang is a citizen of China as well but he is also a citizen of Guyana. He claims to fear persecution in Guyana and that he is a person in need of protection because of his ethnicity.

propositions.text: Ms. Xu and son make similar claims regarding Guyana; Mr. Yang also claims protection in China as spouse of Falun Gong practitioner.
propositions.quote: Ms. Xu and their son make similar claims with respect to Guyana. Mr. Yang also sought protection vis-à-vis China as the spouse of a Falun Gong practitioner.

propositions.text: All three rely on Ms. Xu's personal narrative to support their protection claims.
propositions.quote: All three applicants relied on the personal narrative submitted by Ms. Xu in support of their claims for protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicants' identities and their protection claims based on persecution fears in China and Guyana, relying on Ms. Xu's narrative.

propositions.text: RPD heard claims jointly on May 4, 2017, and rejected them on May 24, 2017 under IRPA sections 96 and 97.
propositions.quote: The claims were heard jointly by the Refugee Protection Division [RPD] of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada [IRB] on May 4, 2017. In a decision dated May 24, 2017, the RPD rejected the claims under both sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.

propositions.text: RPD satisfied applicants established identity and nationality.
propositions.quote: The RPD member was satisfied that the applicants had established their personal identities and nationalities.

propositions.text: RPD found discrimination against Chinese in Guyana but not persecution or protection need for Mr. Yang; risk was generalized violence.
propositions.quote: with respect to Mr. Yang, the member concluded that, while there is some discrimination against Chinese people in Guyana, it did not rise to the level of persecution, nor would circumstances there cause Mr. Yang to be a person in need of protection. At most, he faced a generalized risk of violence.

propositions.text: RPD found Ms. Xu and son had access to Guyanese rights, thus excluded under Article 1E of Refugee Convention.
propositions.quote: with respect to Ms. Xu and her son, the member concluded that, because they “had access to the rights of nationals of Guyana,” they fell within Article 1E of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, 189 UNTS 150 [Refugee Convention] and, therefore, were excluded from refugee protection in Canada.

propositions.text: RPD found no basis to exempt Ms. Xu and son from Article 1E exclusion; applied Mr. Yang's findings to them.
propositions.quote: The member also concluded that there was no basis to exempt them from the application of Article 1E of the Refugee Convention because his findings with respect to Mr. Yang’s claim applied equally to them.

propositions.text: RPD did not address allegations regarding China.
propositions.quote: The member therefore did not address any of the allegations with respect to China.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected claims, finding identity established, no persecution for Mr. Yang in Guyana, and Ms. Xu and son excluded under Article 1E.

propositions.text: Applicants appealed to RAD without new evidence or hearing request.
propositions.quote: The applicants appealed this decision to the Refugee Appeal Division [RAD] of the IRB. They did not file any new evidence or request a hearing.

propositions.text: RAD confirmed RPD decision and dismissed appeal on January 29, 2018.
propositions.quote: In a decision dated January 29, 2018, the RAD confirmed the decision of the RPD and dismissed the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD dismissed the applicants' appeal, confirming the RPD decision without new evidence or hearing.

propositions.text: Applicants argue RAD denied procedural fairness by deciding state protection issue without notice or opportunity to address it.
propositions.quote: They submit that the RAD denied them procedural fairness when it decided the issue of state protection against them without first giving them notice that this issue was in play or an opportunity to address it.

propositions.text: Applicants argue RAD's findings on lack of nexus, risk nature in Guyana, and Article 1E exclusion are unreasonable.
propositions.quote: They also submit that the RAD’s determinations with respect to the lack of nexus to a Convention ground, with respect to the nature of the risk they face in Guyana, and with respect to exclusion under Article 1E of the Refugee Convention, are unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue RAD denied procedural fairness and made unreasonable findings on nexus, risk, and Article 1E exclusion.

propositions.text: Court allows judicial review application due to RAD's unreasonable Article 1E exclusion and procedural fairness breach on state protection.
propositions.quote: For the reasons set out below, I am allowing this application for judicial review. I am satisfied that the RAD’s determination with respect to Article 1E exclusion is unreasonable. I am also satisfied that the RAD’s consideration of the issue of state protection breached the requirements of procedural fairness.

propositions.text: A new hearing is required as a result.
propositions.quote: As a result, a new hearing is required.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows judicial review, finding RAD's Article 1E exclusion unreasonable and procedural fairness breached, requiring a new hearing.

propositions.text: Ms. Xu born in China July 1977; Mr. Yang born China November 1975; son born China August 2003; all Chinese nationals by birth.
propositions.quote: Ms. Xu was born in China in July 1977. Mr. Yang was born there in November 1975. Their son Jie Tao was born there in August 2003. All three are Chinese nationals by birth.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicants' birth dates and Chinese nationality by birth.

propositions.text: Mr. Yang left China in February 2004 to work in Guyana and support family.
propositions.quote: In February 2004, Mr. Yang left China to work in Guyana and support the family.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Yang left China in 2004 to work in Guyana.

propositions.text: Ms. Xu claims medical problems in China due to family planning practices; she joined husband in Guyana in December 2010; son stayed with grandparents in China.
propositions.quote: Ms. Xu claims that after their son was born she faced a number of medical problems in China as a result of Chinese family planning practices and requirements. Eventually, in December 2010 she decided to join her husband in Guyana. Their son remained behind with his grandparents in China.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Xu claims medical problems from family planning in China and joined husband in Guyana in 2010; son stayed in China.

propositions.text: Mr. Yang granted Guyanese citizenship May 2013; bought restaurant; both worked there; restaurant robbed twice; Ms. Xu assaulted; they decided to sell and leave Guyana; Ms. Xu left June 2014; Mr. Yang stayed to sell.
propositions.quote: In May 2013, Mr. Yang was granted Guyanese citizenship. That same month, he bought a restaurant in Georgetown, Guyana. Both he and Ms. Xu worked there. According to Ms. Xu’s narrative, the restaurant was robbed at gunpoint twice – the first time on December 10, 2013; the second time on May 5, 2014. In the first robbery, a gun was put to Ms. Xu’s head and she was assaulted. Shots were fired in the second robbery. After the second robbery, Ms. Xu and Mr. Yang decided to sell the restaurant and leave Guyana. Ms. Xu left for China on June 16, 2014. Mr. Yang stayed behind to sell the restaurant.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Yang became Guyanese citizen, bought restaurant, faced robberies; Ms. Xu assaulted; they decided to sell and leave; Ms. Xu left in 2014.

propositions.text: Ms. Xu claims ongoing family planning difficulties in China; took up Falun Gong; PSB raided session; she escaped and hid; arranged smuggling to US with son; reunited with Mr. Yang; entered Canada irregularly.
propositions.quote: Ms. Xu claims that her difficulties with Chinese family planning practices and requirements continued after she returned to China. On the advice of a cousin, she took up the practice of Falun Gong as a way to deal with these difficulties. However, on August 31, 2014, a Falun Gong group session in which she was participating was raided by the Public Security Bureau [PSB]. Ms. Xu was able to make her escape and went into hiding. Upon learning that the PSB were searching for her, Ms. Xu made arrangements with a smuggler to leave China for the United States with her son. The two of them met up with Mr. Yang in Seattle, Washington, in February 2015. They then all entered Canada irregularly near Vancouver.

propositions.text: Applicants submitted refugee claims in Toronto about one month after entering Canada.
propositions.quote: They submitted their refugee claims in Toronto approximately one month later.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Xu took up Falun Gong, escaped PSB raid, smuggled to US with son, reunited with Mr. Yang, then entered Canada irregularly and claimed refugee status.

propositions.text: Ms. Xu and Mr. Yang submitted Basis of Claim Forms relying on Ms. Xu's narrative; each raised distinct claims re China and Guyana.
propositions.quote: Ms. Xu and Mr. Yang each submitted a Basis of Claim Form and other required documents but both relied on the information set out in Ms. Xu’s narrative. While the factual basis for the claims was advanced in common, each of the applicants raised distinct claims vis-à-vis China and Guyana.

propositions.text: Ms. Xu fears arrest and abuse in China for Falun Gong and forced IUD; fears for son's safety; Mr. Yang fears Guyana due to criminals and China due to Falun Gong; all seek refugee protection.
propositions.quote: In China I fear arrest, imprisonment and abuse by the authorities because of my being a Falun Gong practitioner. I also fear being forced to wear an IUD against my will which I am against. In terms of my son, I fear for his safety as well because of my practice of Falun Gong. My husband too fears living in Guyana where he is worried that he will again be targeted by criminals and gangsters. It is similarly not safe for him to live in China because of my being a Falun Gong practitioner. For these reasons we are all seeking refugee protection in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants submitted claims relying on Ms. Xu's narrative; each fears persecution in China or Guyana and seeks refugee protection.

propositions.text: Applicants' counsel filed written submissions after RPD hearing relying on Ms. Xu's narrative; legal submissions focused on identity, credibility, and exclusion.
propositions.quote: Counsel for the applicants filed written submissions shortly after the hearing before the RPD. Counsel continued to rely on all the grounds identified in Ms. Xu’s narrative. The legal submissions were framed around three specific issues: (1) identity; (2) credibility; and (3) exclusion (“ability of wife and minor son to get status in Guyana”).

propositions.text: RPD member's reasons show no different view of material issues than counsel's submissions.
propositions.quote: There is no suggestion in the RPD member’s reasons that he had a different view of what the material issues in the case were.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants' counsel submitted on identity, credibility, and exclusion; RPD member agreed on material issues.

propositions.text: RPD member satisfied identity established but rejected claims under IRPA sections 96 and 97, limiting analysis to Guyana claims.
propositions.quote: As noted, the RPD member was satisfied that identity had been established. However, the member rejected the claims under both sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA. He limited his analysis to the claims vis-à-vis Guyana.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found identity established but rejected claims, focusing on Guyana.

propositions.text: RPD accepted restaurant robberies occurred but found no future risk engaging sections 96 or 97 for Mr. Yang.
propositions.quote: With respect to Mr. Yang, the member evidently accepted that the restaurant robberies had occurred but found that they were not indicative of a future risk that would engage either section 96 or 97.

propositions.text: Even if robberies were due to ethnicity, risk related to restaurant now sold; no suggestion claimants unsafe in other employment.
propositions.quote: Even if the robberies were “precipitated by” the claimants’ ethnicity, the member found that the risk “was still in relation to the claimants’ restaurant which has now been sold.” In the member’s view, there was “no suggestion or allegation that the claimants would be unable to live safely in Guyana in another employment capacity other than as restaurant owners.”

propositions.text: RPD found some discrimination against ethnic Chinese in Guyana but not persecution; risk was general crime risk; no findings on state protection.
propositions.quote: The member also found that while there is some discrimination against ethnic Chinese in Guyana, it did not rise to the level of persecution nor would Mr. Yang be exposed to anything more than a general risk of being a victim of crime there. The member did not make any findings with respect to state protection.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found robberies occurred but no persecution risk for Mr. Yang; risk was general crime; no state protection findings.

propositions.text: RPD found Tretsetsang case determinative; Ms. Xu and son had access to Guyanese citizenship rights but made no reasonable efforts to obtain it.
propositions.quote: With respect to Ms. Xu and her son, the member found that the decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in Tretsetsang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FCA 175 [Tretsetsang], was “determinative.” In the member’s view, “Guyanese citizenship is within the control of the wife and child, and whereas they have not made any attempts to secure Guyanese citizenship, the panel finds that they have not made any reasonable efforts to overcome whatever impediments there may be, if any would even exist.”

propositions.text: RPD concluded Ms. Xu and son excluded under Article 1E of Refugee Convention and sections 96 and 97 not engaged for them regarding Guyana.
propositions.quote: On this basis, the member concluded that Ms. Xu and her son “have access to the rights of nationals of Guyana as contemplated in Article 1E of the Refugee Convention and they are excluded from refugee consideration in Canada.” Further, the member found that neither sections 96 nor 97 of the IRPA was engaged with respect to Ms. Xu and her son vis-à-vis Guyana.

propositions.text: RPD applied same findings as for Mr. Yang; no evidence Falun Gong practitioners persecuted in Guyana or IUD forced on Ms. Xu there.
propositions.quote: The member applied the same findings as he made with respect to Mr. Yang’s claim and added: “There was no suggestion and no evidence that Falun Gong practitioners are persecuted in Guyana, nor that the wife would be required to wear an IUD in Guyana.” (To be sure, Ms. Xu’s claim for protection was never advanced on this basis.)

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Ms. Xu and son excluded under Article 1E due to access to Guyanese rights; no persecution or forced IUD claims in Guyana.

propositions.text: Applicants' appeal to RAD focused on three issues: RPD error on nexus to Convention ground, generalized risk in Guyana, and Article 1E exclusion for Ms. Xu and son.
propositions.quote: In their written submissions in support of the appeal, the applicants identified and directed their submissions to the following three issues: a) Did the RPD err in finding that there is no nexus between Mr. Yang’s fear and a Convention ground? b) Did the RPD err in finding that Mr. Yang only faces a generalized risk in Guyana? c) Did the RPD err in finding that Ms. Xu and Jie Tao are excluded from protection pursuant to Article 1E of the Refugee Convention?

paragraphs.summary: Applicants appealed to RAD arguing RPD erred on nexus, risk, and Article 1E exclusion issues.

propositions.text: Minister did not participate in the appeal.
propositions.quote: The Minister did not participate in the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Minister did not participate in the appeal.

propositions.text: RAD instructed by Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica and RAD panel in X (Re) to apply correctness standard to RPD findings of fact and mixed fact and law.
propositions.quote: In his reasons for dismissing the appeal, the RAD member instructed himself in accordance with the decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93 [Huruglica] as well as the decision of the three member RAD panel in X (Re), 2017 CanLII 33034 (CA IRB). As the member understood these authorities, with respect to findings of fact and mixed fact and law he was “to review the RPD decisions applying the correctness standard.

propositions.text: RAD conducts own analysis to determine if RPD erred; may apply reasonableness standard if RPD has meaningful advantage.
propositions.quote: Thus, after carefully considering the RPD’s decision, the RAD carries out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the Appellant, the RPD erred.” While the member does not say so expressly, it must be presumed that he also followed the direction of the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica (as elaborated upon by the three member panel of the RAD) that the RAD will normally apply a standard of correctness to all the findings of the RPD but where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage over the RAD in making a particular finding, the RAD may assess that finding using a standard of reasonableness, modified to suit the RAD context.

propositions.text: None of the grounds of appeal were decided on reasonableness standard; credibility was not an issue.
propositions.quote: As it happened, none of the grounds of appeal were determined on this basis. Credibility was not an issue.

paragraphs.summary: RAD applied correctness standard to RPD findings per Huruglica; no grounds decided on reasonableness; credibility not at issue.

propositions.text: RAD dismissed the appeal for reasons set out in following paragraphs.
propositions.quote: The RAD dismissed the appeal for the following reasons.

paragraphs.summary: RAD dismissed the appeal for reasons to follow.

propositions.text: RAD found RPD's statement on robberies and ethnicity less clear but rejected applicants' claim of ethnic risk in Guyana.
propositions.quote: First, while the RAD found that the RPD member’s statement that “[e]ven if the robberies were precipitated by the claimants’ ethnicity, it was still in relation to the claimants’ restaurant which has now been sold” was less clear than it could have been, the RAD rejected the applicants’ contention that they were at risk in Guyana, whether they were restaurant owners or not, because of their ethnicity.

propositions.text: RAD reviewed documentary evidence and concluded applicants failed to establish well-founded fear of targeting on Convention ground.
propositions.quote: The RAD member conducted his own review of the documentary evidence before the RPD regarding country conditions in Guyana and concluded that the applicants had failed to establish a well-founded fear that they would be targeted on a Convention ground.

propositions.text: RAD agreed with RPD that applicants failed to establish nexus between fears and Convention ground.
propositions.quote: In short, the RAD agreed with the RPD that the applicants had failed to establish a nexus between their fears and a Convention ground.

paragraphs.summary: RAD found RPD's ethnic risk statement unclear but rejected ethnic risk claim; agreed applicants failed to establish nexus to Convention ground.

propositions.text: The RAD member considered whether applicants personally faced a unique risk under IRPA s 97(1)(b)(ii).
propositions.quote: the determinative issue was whether the applicants personally faced a risk that “is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country” (IRPA, s 97(1)(b)(ii))

propositions.text: The RAD member reviewed evidence including state protection in Guyana and concluded applicants' fear of crime is a general risk in Guyana.
propositions.quote: the applicants’ fear of crime “is a risk faced generally by others in Guyana”

propositions.text: Applicants had not rebutted presumption that state protection is unavailable in Guyana.
propositions.quote: applicants had “not rebutted the presumption that state protection is not [sic] available to them in Guyana.”

propositions.text: RAD member agreed with RPD that evidence does not support applicants were specifically targeted due to Chinese ethnicity and protection is unavailable.
propositions.quote: the evidence does not support the Appellants’ allegations that they were specifically targeted by criminals in Guyana because of their Chinese ethnicity and that protection is not available to them.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD member found applicants' fear of crime is a general risk in Guyana and agreed with RPD that applicants were not specifically targeted and state protection is unavailable.

propositions.text: RAD member agreed with RPD that Mr. Yang is excluded from refugee protection under Article 1E of the Refugee Convention.
propositions.quote: he agreed with the assessment of the RPD that Mr. Yang “is excluded from refugee protection under Article 1E” of the Refugee Convention.

propositions.text: RAD member found Ms. Xu and her son have access to rights of Guyana nationals under Article 1E and are excluded from refugee consideration in Canada.
propositions.quote: [Ms. Xu and her son] have access to the rights of nationals of Guyana as contemplated in Article 1E of the Convention and they are excluded from refugee consideration in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD member agreed with RPD that Mr. Yang is excluded under Article 1E and that Ms. Xu and her son have rights in Guyana and are excluded from refugee consideration.

propositions.text: RAD confirmed RPD decision under IRPA s 111(1)(a) and dismissed the appeal.
propositions.quote: the RAD confirmed the decision of the RPD under section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA and dismissed the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD confirmed the RPD decision and dismissed the appeal under IRPA s 111(1)(a).

propositions.text: RAD's factual and mixed fact-law determinations are reviewed on a reasonableness standard.
propositions.quote: The RAD’s determinations of factual issues and issues of mixed fact and law are reviewed on a reasonableness standard (Huruglica at para 35).

propositions.text: Reasonableness review concerns substantive outcome and articulation process.
propositions.quote: Reasonableness review “is concerned with the reasonableness of the substantive outcome of the decision, and with the process of articulating that outcome” (Canada (Attorney General) v Igloo Vikski Inc, 2016 SCC 38 at para 18).

propositions.text: Reviewing court must look at outcome and reasons given for it.
propositions.quote: the reviewing court must look at both the outcome and the reasons that are given for that outcome (Delta Air Lines Inc v Lukács, 2018 SCC 2 at para 27).

propositions.text: Court examines decision for justification, transparency, intelligibility and whether it falls within acceptable outcomes.
propositions.quote: The reviewing court examines the decision for “the existence of justification, transparency and intelligibility within the decision-making process” and determines “whether the decision falls within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and law” (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 47).

propositions.text: Reasons must allow court to understand decision and determine if conclusion is acceptable.
propositions.quote: These criteria are met if “the reasons allow the reviewing court to understand why the tribunal made its decision and permit it to determine whether the conclusion is within the range of acceptable outcomes” (Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses’ Union v Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62 at para 16).

propositions.text: Court should intervene only if criteria not met; not to reweigh evidence or substitute view.
propositions.quote: The reviewing court should intervene only if these criteria are not met. It is not the role of the reviewing court to reweigh the evidence or to substitute its own view of a preferable outcome (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at paras 59 and 61 [Khosa]).

paragraphs.summary: The reasonableness standard requires reviewing court to assess outcome and reasons, intervening only if decision lacks justification or intelligibility.

propositions.text: No standard of review applies to procedural fairness issues; court decides fairness itself.
propositions.quote: if the issue is whether there was a breach of procedural fairness before the RAD, no standard of review is engaged. Rather, the reviewing court must determine for itself whether the process the member followed satisfied the level of fairness required in all the circumstances (Khosa at para 43; Canadian Pacific Railway Co v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 at para 54).

paragraphs.summary: Procedural fairness issues are reviewed on a correctness basis; court decides fairness itself without standard of review.

propositions.text: Is RAD's Article 1E exclusion determination unreasonable?
propositions.quote: Is the RAD’s determination that the applicants are excluded from refugee protection in Canada because of Article 1E of the Refugee Convention unreasonable?

propositions.text: Did RAD deny procedural fairness by deciding state protection issue without notice or opportunity to address?
propositions.quote: Did the RAD deny the applicants procedural fairness by deciding the issue of state protection against them without first giving them notice that this issue was in play or an opportunity to address it?

propositions.text: Is RAD's conclusion that applicants failed to establish well-founded fear of persecution unreasonable?
propositions.quote: Is the RAD’s conclusion that the applicants failed to establish that they had a well-founded fear of persecution in Guyana unreasonable?

propositions.text: Is RAD's conclusion that applicants failed to establish need for protection unreasonable?
propositions.quote: Is the RAD’s conclusion that the applicants failed to establish that they were persons in need of protection in Guyana unreasonable?

paragraphs.summary: Court frames four issues: Article 1E exclusion, procedural fairness on state protection, well-founded fear of persecution, and need for protection.

propositions.text: Applicants did not present grounds in this order; first two issues are determinative; others need not be addressed.
propositions.quote: I have found the first two of these issues to be determinative of this application. It is therefore not necessary to address the other two issues.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds first two issues determinative and will not address the other two.

propositions.text: Before addressing grounds, court reviews RAD's role briefly.
propositions.quote: Before addressing the grounds of judicial review set out above, it may be helpful to review the role of the RAD briefly.

paragraphs.summary: Court introduces a brief review of the RAD's role before analysis.

propositions.text: IRPA s 110(1) allows appeal to RAD on law, fact or mixed fact-law questions from RPD decisions.
propositions.quote: Section 110(1) of the IRPA provides that a person or the Minister “may appeal, in accordance with the rules of the Board, on a question of law, of fact or of mixed fact and law, to the Refugee Appeal Division against a decision of the Refugee Protection Division to allow or reject the person’s claim for refugee protection.”

propositions.text: IRPA s 110(2) limits appeals to RAD in certain cases but no other ground limitations where appeal exists.
propositions.quote: Section 110(2) provides that there is no appeal to the RAD in certain classes of cases; however, where there is a right of appeal to the RAD, no other limitations are placed on the grounds of appeal that may be advanced.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains IRPA provisions allowing appeals to RAD on law, fact, or mixed questions with some limitations.

propositions.text: IRPA s 110(3) requires RAD appeals to proceed without hearing, based on RPD record.
propositions.quote: Section 110(3) of the IRPA provides that generally an appeal to the RAD “must proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the record of the proceedings of the Refugee Protection Division.”

propositions.text: IRPA ss 110(4)-(6) allow exceptions for new evidence and hearings under conditions.
propositions.quote: Sections 110(4) and (5), which govern the admission of new evidence from the person who is the subject of the appeal, create an exception to this general rule. So too does section 110(6), which permits the RAD to hold a hearing provided certain preconditions are met.

propositions.text: FCA in Singh explained restrictions on new evidence preserve process integrity and finality at first decision level.
propositions.quote: placing restrictions on the admissibility of new evidence on appeal helps to preserve the integrity of the process by promoting finality with respect to the factual record at the first level of decision-making (with limited exceptions) and encouraging the narrowing of issues as matters move up the appellate ladder (at paras 43 and 50).

paragraphs.summary: Court explains RAD appeals proceed without hearing on RPD record, with exceptions for new evidence and hearings, citing FCA in Singh.

propositions.text: RAD appeal is not a true de novo proceeding; it reviews RPD decision and conducts own analysis of record.
propositions.quote: An appeal to the RAD is not a true de novo proceeding (Huruglica at para 79). The RAD conducts an appeal of the RPD’s decision, which is the initial point of reference. It does so generally on the basis of the evidentiary record that was before the RPD. After “carefully considering” the RPD’s decision, the RAD should carry out “its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the appellant, the RPD erred” (Huruglica at para 103).

paragraphs.summary: RAD appeals are not de novo but review RPD decisions and analyze record to determine errors.

propositions.text: RAD has broad mandate to correct RPD errors of fact, law, or mixed fact-law; reviews RPD findings on correctness standard.
propositions.quote: The RAD has a broad mandate to intervene to correct any error of fact, law, or mixed fact and law made by the RPD (Huruglica at paras 78 and 103). The RAD reviews the RPD’s findings on the standard of correctness, although it may defer to the RPD on credibility findings “where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage” (Huruglica at para 70).

propositions.text: RAD may confirm, set aside, substitute, or refer RPD decisions under IRPA s 111(1) and (2).
propositions.quote: After considering the appeal, the RAD may confirm the determination of the RPD; it may set aside the determination of the RPD and substitute a determination that, in its opinion, should have been made; or it may refer the matter to the RPD for a redetermination (but only if it has found that the RPD has erred but the RAD cannot decide whether to confirm the determination of the RPD or substitute a different one without hearing the evidence that was presented to the RPD) (IRPA, s 111(1) and (2)).

paragraphs.summary: RAD can correct RPD errors, review on correctness standard, and confirm, set aside, substitute, or refer decisions under IRPA.

propositions.text: RAD can confirm RPD decision on another basis but must respect natural justice and procedural fairness.
propositions.quote: If there is an error, the RAD can still confirm the decision of the RPD on another basis (Huruglica at para 78). Nevertheless, this power must be exercised in accordance with the principles of natural justice and procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Before confirming on a basis outside framed issues, RAD must give notice and opportunity to make submissions.
propositions.quote: before confirming a decision of the RPD on a basis that cannot reasonably be said to stem from the issues as framed by the parties, the RAD must give the affected parties notice and an opportunity to make submissions (Ching v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 725 at paras 65-76; Ojarikre v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 896 at paras 20-23; Kwakwa v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 600 at paras 24-26; Tan v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 876 at para 40).

propositions.text: If RAD makes further substantive findings, it should give notice and opportunity to parties.
propositions.quote: if the RAD chooses to take a frolic and venture into the record to make further substantive findings, it should give some sort of notice to the parties and give them an opportunity to make submissions” (Husian v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 684 at para 10).

paragraphs.summary: RAD must give notice and opportunity to parties before confirming RPD decision on new bases or making further substantive findings.

propositions.text: Article 1E excludes persons recognized by competent authorities as having rights and obligations of nationality in that country.
propositions.quote: Article 1E of the Refugee Convention states: “This Convention shall not apply to a person who is recognized by the competent authorities of the country in which he has taken residence as having the rights and obligations which are attached to the possession of nationality in that country.”

paragraphs.summary: Article 1E excludes persons recognized by competent authorities as having rights and obligations of nationality in that country.

propositions.text: RAD member's conclusions on Article 1E are puzzling in at least two respects.
propositions.quote: the RAD member’s conclusions with respect to the application of Article 1E in the present case are puzzling in at least two respects.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD member's Article 1E conclusions puzzling in two respects.

propositions.text: RAD member finds Mr. Yang excluded under Article 1E, apparently agreeing with RPD, but RPD made no such finding.
propositions.quote: the RAD member is expressing agreement with the RPD member’s conclusion in this regard. However, the RPD member drew no such conclusion with respect to Mr. Yang.

propositions.text: Issue of Article 1E exclusion for Mr. Yang is a red herring; he sought protection for China and Guyana under IRPA s 96(a).
propositions.quote: the issue of the applicability of Article 1E to Mr. Yang would appear to be a red herring. He was seeking refugee protection vis-à-vis two different countries of which he is a national – China and Guyana.

propositions.text: Under IRPA s 96(a), burden is on claimant to show well-founded fear of persecution in each country of nationality.
propositions.quote: Under section 96(a) of the IRPA, the burden was on him to demonstrate a well-founded fear of persecution in relation to both of these countries of citizenship before he could seek asylum in Canada (cf. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Williams, 2005 FCA 126 at para 20).

propositions.text: Article 1E exclusion has nothing to do with Mr. Yang's burden under s 96(a).
propositions.quote: This has nothing to do with Article 1E exclusion.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD's Article 1E exclusion of Mr. Yang puzzling and irrelevant given s 96(a) burden to show fear of persecution in both countries.

propositions.text: RAD member states Ms. Xu and son have rights of Guyana nationals under Article 1E and are excluded from refugee consideration.
propositions.quote: he finds “as did the RPD that [Ms. Xu and her son], have access to the rights of nationals of Guyana as contemplated in Article 1E of the Convention and they are excluded from refugee consideration in Canada.”

propositions.text: RPD found Ms. Xu and son excluded under Article 1E on erroneous basis relying on Tretsetsang case.
propositions.quote: the RPD member found that Ms. Xu and her son were excluded under Article 1E, he did so on what is clearly an erroneous basis. As noted above, the RPD member considered the decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in Tretsetsang to be “determinative on this point.”

propositions.text: Tretsetsang concerns meaning of 'each of their countries of nationality' in IRPA s 96(a), not Article 1E.
propositions.quote: Tretsetsang, however, concerns the meaning of “each of their countries of nationality” in section 96(a) of the IRPA, not Article 1E of the Refugee Convention.

propositions.text: RAD member does not mention RPD's flawed analysis but may have done own analysis under Zeng test, which is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The RAD member does not mention this flaw in the RPD’s analysis, although perhaps it is why he went on to conduct his own analysis under the proper test, as stated in Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Zeng, 2010 FCA 118 [Zeng]. As I will explain, however, that analysis is unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RPD's Article 1E exclusion of Ms. Xu and son based on Tretsetsang is erroneous; RAD's own analysis under Zeng is unreasonable.

propositions.text: Zeng test for Article 1E exclusion: does claimant have status similar to nationals in third country? If yes, excluded; if no, consider loss of status and other factors.
propositions.quote: In Zeng, the Federal Court of Appeal formulated the test for exclusion under Article 1E of the Refugee Convention as follows (at para 28): Considering all relevant factors to the date of the hearing, does the claimant have status, substantially similar to that of its nationals, in the third country? If the answer is yes, the claimant is excluded. If the answer is no, the next question is whether the claimant previously had such status and lost it, or had access to such status and failed to acquire it. If the answer is no, the claimant is not excluded under Article 1E. If the answer is yes, the RPD must consider and balance various factors. These include, but are not limited to, the reason for the loss of status (voluntary or involuntary), whether the claimant could return to the third country, the risk the claimant would face in the home country, Canada’s international obligations, and any other relevant facts.

paragraphs.summary: Zeng test for Article 1E exclusion considers claimant's status in third country and factors if status lost or not acquired.

propositions.text: Court understands RAD member answered Zeng test questions in a certain way.
propositions.quote: As I understand the RAD member’s reasons, he answered these questions in the following way.

paragraphs.summary: Court introduces its understanding of how RAD member applied Zeng test.

propositions.text: RAD member found Ms. Xu and son did not have status substantially similar to nationals in Guyana at hearing time, so not excluded on that basis.
propositions.quote: First, neither Ms. Xu nor her son had status in Guyana substantially similar to that of its nationals at the time of the hearing. They were therefore not excluded from refugee protection on this basis.

paragraphs.summary: RAD member found Ms. Xu and son lacked status similar to Guyana nationals and thus not excluded on that basis.

propositions.text: RAD member could not conclude Ms. Xu and son had status, though Ms. Xu had right to reside in Guyana then
propositions.quote: the RAD member was unable to conclude that Ms. Xu and her son ever had such status although it was clear that Ms. Xu (at least) had had a right to reside in Guyana during the time she was there.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD member found Ms. Xu and her son did not have status, though Ms. Xu had right to reside in Guyana then.

propositions.text: Applicants had access to status similar to Guyanese nationals when Ms. Xu lived with Mr. Yang 2010-2014
propositions.quote: they did have access to status substantially similar to that of nationals of Guyana – in particular, when Ms. Xu was living there with Mr. Yang between December 2010 and June 2014.

propositions.text: Ms. Xu aware she could apply for status but took no action to normalize it
propositions.quote: she was aware of her ability to apply for status in Guyana, but she took no action or made any attempt to normalize her status

propositions.text: Ms. Xu failed without good reason to preserve right to return to Guyana
propositions.quote: she failed “without good and sufficient reason” to preserve her right to be permitted to return to Guyana

propositions.text: Ms. Xu and son excluded from refugee protection under Article 1E of Refugee Convention
propositions.quote: he concluded that Ms. Xu and her son were excluded from refugee protection under Article 1E of the Refugee Convention.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found applicants had similar status to nationals but Ms. Xu did not normalize it and was excluded from refugee protection under Article 1E.

propositions.text: Applicants challenged RPD finding that Guyanese citizenship was within their control
propositions.quote: the applicants specifically took issue with the RPD member’s finding that Guyanese citizenship was “within the control” of Ms. Xu and her son

propositions.text: Canadian case law holds potential Guyanese citizenship not within spouse's control as it is discretionary executive decision
propositions.quote: Canadian case law dealing specifically with Guyana which holds that potential Guyanese citizenship is not “within the control” of the spouse of a Guyanese citizen because whether it is granted or not is determined by the Executive in the exercise of its discretion

propositions.text: Evidence before RAD suggested discretion still applies but member did not address applicants' argument
propositions.quote: The evidence before the RAD suggested that this was still the case but the member does not address the applicants’ argument.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants challenged RPD's control finding; case law says citizenship is discretionary; RAD did not address this argument.

propositions.text: Whether case law on section 96(a) IRPA fits Zeng test is not determinative here
propositions.quote: I do not need to determine how this case law, which pertains to section 96(a) of the IRPA, fits in the Zeng test, if at all.

propositions.text: RAD failed to consider Ms. Xu's explanation for not securing status in Guyana before seeking Canada protection
propositions.quote: the determinative issue here is the failure of the RAD member to engage in any meaningful way with Ms. Xu’s explanation for why she did not attempt to secure her status in Guyana

propositions.text: Ms. Xu left Guyana after two violent armed robberies and feared further victimization
propositions.quote: Ms. Xu left Guyana because she had been the victim of two violent armed robberies within less than six months. She feared being a victim again.

propositions.text: RPD and RAD did not disbelieve Ms. Xu's account of robberies but found it insufficient for claims under sections 96 or 97 IRPA
propositions.quote: Neither the RPD nor the RAD member disbelieved Ms. Xu’s account of these events. Even assuming, as the RPD and the RAD concluded, that these experiences were insufficient to establish her claims under sections 96 or 97 of the IRPA

propositions.text: Under Zeng, Ms. Xu's explanation for losing status must be considered but RAD did not do so
propositions.quote: Under Zeng, Ms. Xu’s explanation for why she lost her status in Guyana must be considered but the member never does so.

propositions.text: RAD's exclusion conclusion under Article 1E lacks justification, transparency and intelligibility
propositions.quote: his conclusion that she is excluded from refugee protection under Article 1E of the Refugee Convention lacks justification, transparency and intelligibility.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD failed to consider Ms. Xu's explanation for status loss, making exclusion under Article 1E unjustified and unclear.

propositions.text: Applicants argued RPD erred on risk nexus and personalized risk under sections 96 and 97 IRPA
propositions.quote: applicants challenged the RPD’s determinations that any risk they faced in Guyana lacked a nexus to a Convention ground, as required by section 96 of the IRPA, and, further, that it did not rise to the level of a personalized risk, as required by section 97.

propositions.text: RAD upheld RPD's determinations but relied on evidence about Guyanese authorities' protection efforts
propositions.quote: the RAD relied on evidence in the record relating to efforts by the authorities in Guyana to protect ethnic Chinese there and made specific findings with respect to state protection.

propositions.text: Applicants say procedural fairness breached as they had no notice or chance to address state protection issue
propositions.quote: The applicants submit that this breached the duty of procedural fairness because they did not have notice that this issue was in play or an opportunity to make submissions with respect to it.

propositions.text: Court agrees applicants were denied procedural fairness on state protection issue
propositions.quote: I agree with the applicants.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argued procedural fairness breached on state protection issue; court agrees with applicants.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness requires notice and opportunity to address new issues before RAD confirms RPD decision on new basis
propositions.quote: the duty of procedural fairness requires that before the RAD confirms a decision of the RPD on a new basis, the party or parties to the appeal must be told that the issue is in play and given an opportunity make submissions on it.

propositions.text: No dispute on principle or test for 'newness' but disputes arise on application in cases
propositions.quote: There does not appear to be any disagreement in the jurisprudence about this principle or about the test for “newness” – i.e. that the issue cannot reasonably be said to stem from the issues as framed by the parties.

paragraphs.summary: Court states procedural fairness requires notice and chance to address new issues; principle undisputed but application varies.

propositions.text: Issue of state protection is new as it was not identified or addressed by RPD or applicants
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that the issue of state protection is a new one in the requisite sense in this case.

propositions.text: Claimants must approach home state for protection before other states' responsibility engaged (Ward)
propositions.quote: persecuted persons are required to approach their home state for protection before the responsibility of other states is engaged (Canada (Attorney General) v Ward, [1993] 2 SCR 689 at 709 [Ward])

propositions.text: Home state's inability to protect is crucial to well-founded fear (Ward)
propositions.quote: their home state’s inability to protect “is a crucial element in determining whether the claimant’s fear is well-founded” (Ward at 722).

propositions.text: State protection was not a material issue at RPD hearing; applicants did not address it; RPD made no determinations on it
propositions.quote: state protection was not identified as a material issue in this case at the hearing before the RPD, as a result the applicants’ written submissions to the RPD do not address it, and the RPD member did not make any determinations in relation to it.

propositions.text: Applicants' appeal to RAD focused on lack of nexus to Convention ground, not state protection
propositions.quote: the applicants’ appeal was understandably – indeed, necessarily – directed to other issues. In particular, in relation to section 96, the issue was the RPD’s finding of a lack of nexus to a Convention ground.

propositions.text: RPD never reached question of whether applicants' fear was well-founded engaging state protection
propositions.quote: The question of whether the applicants’ subjective fear was well-founded in the sense that engages state protection was never reached by the RPD.

propositions.text: State protection issue did not stem from issues framed by applicants and they had no reason to expect it
propositions.quote: the issue of state protection cannot reasonably be said to stem from the issues as framed by the applicants in their appeal to the RAD and they had no reason to think that it would become an issue.

propositions.text: Applicants were entitled to notice and opportunity to make submissions on state protection before RAD decision
propositions.quote: they were entitled to be told that state protection was in play at the RAD and they should have had an opportunity to make submissions on it before the appeal was decided.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds state protection issue was new, not addressed by RPD or applicants, so applicants deserved notice and chance to respond.

propositions.text: Respondent says state protection issue is immaterial as RAD could uphold RPD decision without it
propositions.quote: the respondent submits, in effect, that even if this is so, the issue of state protection is immaterial in this case because it is really only an alternative basis for upholding the RPD’s decision

propositions.text: RAD had other reasons unrelated to state protection to uphold RPD determinations without error
propositions.quote: some of the reasons the RAD offered for upholding the RPD’s determinations have nothing whatsoever to do with state protection and those reasons are not tainted by any other reviewable error.

propositions.text: Adverse outcome was legally inevitable despite procedural fairness breach (citing Marin)
propositions.quote: According to the respondent, an adverse outcome for the applicants was legally inevitable (cf. Marin v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 243 at paras 39-40 and the cases cited therein).

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues state protection issue immaterial and adverse outcome inevitable despite fairness breach.

propositions.text: Court not persuaded to overlook procedural fairness breach due to legal inevitability
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded that the breach of procedural fairness should be overlooked because the result in this case was legally inevitable.

propositions.text: Court gives three main reasons for rejecting legal inevitability argument
propositions.quote: I say this for three main reasons.

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects respondent's legal inevitability argument and will explain three reasons.

propositions.text: Breach relates to claims vis-à-vis Guyana but claims vis-à-vis China never examined on merits due to exclusion under Article 1E
propositions.quote: the applicants had also made claims vis-à-vis China. These claims have never been examined on their merits because of erroneous determinations that Ms. Xu was excluded under Article 1E.

propositions.text: Court cannot say claims are doomed to fail after proper consideration
propositions.quote: I am in no position to say that her claim for protection is doomed to fail in its entirety after proper consideration.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes claims regarding China were never examined and cannot say they will fail after proper review.

propositions.text: State protection issue intertwined with RAD's section 97 determination relying on presumption of state protection
propositions.quote: I am not satisfied that the issue of state protection can safely be disentangled from the rest of the RAD member’s reasons in this case.

propositions.text: RAD member found applicants did not rebut presumption of state protection without submissions from applicants
propositions.quote: The member expressly makes and relies upon the finding that the applicants have not rebutted the presumption that state protection is available to them in Guyana.

propositions.text: Upholding result on respondent's basis would require rewriting RAD reasons, exceeding judicial review bounds
propositions.quote: To uphold the result on the basis advanced by the respondent would require fundamentally re-writing the member’s reasons, something that exceeds the proper bounds of judicial review in the circumstances of this case.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds state protection issue integral to RAD's reasoning and rewriting reasons exceeds judicial review scope.

propositions.text: State protection important to RAD's section 96 reasoning on nexus with Convention ground
propositions.quote: state protection is less prominent in the member’s discussion under section 96 of the IRPA, it is important nonetheless and relates directly to the issue of nexus with a Convention ground.

propositions.text: RAD diminished probative value of applicants' news reports due to missing context of Guyanese authorities' protection efforts
propositions.quote: A key reason the member gave for upholding the finding of a lack of nexus was that the probative value of information the applicants drew from two news reports ... was diminished because the applicants had taken that information “out of context.”

propositions.text: RPD did not rely on information about Guyanese authorities' protection efforts
propositions.quote: The RPD member had not placed any reliance on this information.

propositions.text: Applicants had no reason to address significance of state protection info until RAD reasons received, which was too late
propositions.quote: The applicants had no reason to think that its significance for their appeal needed to be addressed until they received the RAD member’s reasons. By then, of course, it was too late.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds state protection issue important to RAD's nexus reasoning and applicants had no chance to address it before decision.

propositions.text: Applicants entitled to submissions on state protection issue before RAD decision; failure breached procedural fairness
propositions.quote: The applicants should have been given an opportunity to make submissions on this issue before the appeal was decided. The failure to do so resulted in a breach of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes failure to allow submissions on state protection breached procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Judicial review application allowed, RAD decision set aside, matter remitted to different decision-maker
propositions.quote: the application for judicial review of the decision of the RAD dated January 29, 2018, is allowed, the decision is set aside, and the matter is remitted for redetermination by a different decision-maker.

paragraphs.summary: Court allows judicial review, sets aside RAD decision, and remits matter for redetermination by different decision-maker.

propositions.text: No serious questions of general importance for certification under section 74(d) IRPA
propositions.quote: The parties did not suggest any serious questions of general importance for certification under section 74(d) of the IRPA. I agree that none arise.

propositions.text: Judgment: judicial review allowed, RAD decision set aside, matter remitted, no question of general importance
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is allowed. The decision of the Refugee Appeal Division dated January 29, 2018, is set aside and the matter is remitted for redetermination by a different decision-maker. No question of general importance is stated.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no questions of general importance and formally orders judicial review allowed, decision set aside, matter remitted.
